title: How do you solve an M&A case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete M&A case guide: standalone value, synergies, integration cost and price, worked through a $60M bakery acquisition, plus mistakes and practice.
hook: Acquisition cases sound technical, but most come down to one comparison: is the company worth more to us than we would pay for it? This guide shows that comparison with real numbers, and how a small change in one assumption can flip the answer.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

A company buying another company (mergers and acquisitions).

The structure

Why buy: growth, capabilities, cost savings or a new market?
  • Is the target good on its own?
    • Its market
    • Its performance vs peers
    • Standalone value (cash flows (DCF) · multiples)
  • What extra is it worth to us?
    • Revenue synergies
    • Cost synergies
    • Minus integration costs
  • Can we make it work?
    • Funding the deal
    • Integration and culture
    • Regulation (competition law)
  • Is the price right?
    • Price vs value to us
    • Alternatives (other targets · build or partner)

Buy only if standalone value + synergies − integration costs is more than the price, and buying beats building it yourself.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a bakery chain can buy a smaller rival for $60M. Should it?

Step 1: standalone value. The rival makes $5M profit a year. Similar businesses sell for about 10 times profit, so it is worth about $50M on its own. The price is already $10M above that.

Step 2: synergies. Sharing bakeries and buying flour together could save $2M a year. At the same 10× multiple, that is worth $20M.

Step 3: integration cost. Merging systems, closing a site and redundancies cost about $6M once.

Step 4: value to us. $50M + $20M − $6M = $64M, against a $60M price. Yes, but only just.

Step 5: test the risk. If only half the synergies arrive, value is $50M + $10M − $6M = $54M, below the price. The deal depends entirely on delivering the savings.

Recommendation: "I'd recommend buying, but only with protection: at $60M we are paying for synergies we have to create ourselves. I'd negotiate the price towards $55M or ask for part of it as an earn-out, and plan the bakery consolidation before signing."

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Valuing the target and stopping, without comparing value to the price.
  2. Counting synergies but forgetting the one-off cost of integration.
  3. Not testing what happens if synergies come in lower, which is common.
  4. Ignoring alternatives: building it ourselves, partnering, or buying a different target.

Phrases to use

Standalone, it is worth about $50M, so at $60M we are paying $10M for synergies. Let's see if they are worth more than that.
The answer is sensitive to synergies: at half the savings, the deal destroys value.

Practise with these prompts

Should a regional bakery chain buy a smaller rival for $60M?

Show a model structure
  • Target on its own: Its profits and growth; Value vs the $60M price
  • Synergies: Cost synergies: shared bakeries, buying, overheads; Revenue synergies: new regions, cross-selling
  • Risks: Integration, staff, customers lost; What we don't know: debts, contracts
  • Alternatives: Grow on our own; Buy a different target

Where to start: Standalone value vs price: synergies should be the bonus, not the reason.

The trap: Paying for synergies the buyer would have to deliver itself.

How would you value a football club for a potential buyer?

Show a model structure
  • Revenue: Media rights, match-day, commercial; Which are contracted vs at risk (relegation)
  • Costs: Player wages and transfers; Stadium, staff; net debt and squad value
  • Value methods: Multiples of recent club deals; Cash-flow value
  • Strategic premium: Brand, stadium, land; What this buyer can add

Where to start: Revenue and how safe it is: media money depends on staying in the league.

The trap: Using one method only; club deals rarely match cash-flow values.

Should a coffee chain buy its main coffee roaster?

Show a model structure
  • Value of the roaster: Its profits, other customers; Price vs value
  • Benefits to us: Lower cost of beans, security of supply; Quality control
  • Risks: Losing the roaster's other customers; Running a factory, a new skill
  • Alternatives: Long-term contract; Minority stake

Where to start: Alternatives: a long contract may give most of the benefit without buying.

The trap: Assuming owning it is the only way to secure supply.

Keep going

  • The framework on its own
  • The quick version: first question and trap
  • More practice prompts in this area

Do not confuse enterprise value with what shareholders receive

Imagine a buyer considering a regional repair business. Comparable firms trade at six times EBITDA and the target earns £4 million EBITDA. That suggests £24 million enterprise value as an initial market reference. If the target has £7 million of financial debt and £2 million of excess cash, indicative equity value is £19 million (£24 million minus debt plus excess cash), before deal-specific adjustments.

The buyer expects £1.2 million annual cost synergies but must invest £3 million integrating systems and sites. The financial value of those synergies depends on when they arrive, whether they recur, and the discount rate. It would be wrong to add £1.2 million directly to a £24 million valuation as though annual savings and present value used the same units.

Suppose, purely for practice, the buyer values sustainable after-tax synergies at eight times the annual after-tax savings. At a 25% illustrative tax rate, £1.2 million pre-tax becomes £0.9 million after tax; eight times gives £7.2 million. Deducting £3 million integration cost leaves roughly £4.2 million of incremental value, before execution risk. This estimate is deliberately simplified, not a full discounted cash-flow model.

The decisive question is who captures the synergy. If competing bidders pay the entire synergy value to the seller, the acquirer gains little. In your final recommendation, give a maximum justifiable price range, the assumptions behind it, the integration risks and a concrete alternative such as a commercial partnership.
